extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political theory, policymakers, and the informed public
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for evaluating democratic governments’ finances, corruption, capacity for sustained effort, self-control, foreign policy, and long-term advantages as discussed in a political-theory text (Alexis de Tocqueville).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparability of public finances between countries
rubrics_metrics.description: It is difficult to compare the expenditure of the Union with that of France because municipal organization, the elements composing budgets, and the allocation of expenses differ (e.g., townships vs Departments, turnpikes vs free roads). A fair comparison cannot be instituted when the elements of the budgets always differ more or less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing national expenditures account for differences in subnational organization, which items are charged to state vs municipal budgets, and the heterogeneity of municipal bodies across regions (e.g., New England vs Georgia). Avoid simplistic one-to-one comparisons when underlying budget components are not analogous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include non-monetary/personal services in expenditure accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments demand not only money but personal services (e.g., soldiers give up time, militia service), which are equivalent to a sum and weigh upon citizens; these must be considered when estimating relative expenditures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and attempt to value services-in-kind and time contributions (militia duty, conscription effects) alongside monetary outlays. Note the difficulty of accurately estimating and comparing these across countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for differing institutional obligations and contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Different governments contract obligations that do not exist elsewhere (e.g., French government pays the clergy; in America the voluntary principle prevails; in America legal provision for the poor exists but in France charity predominates; public officers paid by fixed salary vs perquisites).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing public expenditure include peculiar national obligations (state-funded clergy, poor relief systems, salary vs perquisites, tolls/turnpikes vs free roads) because they profoundly affect apparent levels of taxation and spending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware false precision in statistical comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: When statistics are not based upon computations which are strictly accurate, they mislead instead of guiding aright; the mind is easily imposed upon by the false affectation of exactness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on crude numerical investigations without strictly accurate computations. Prefer qualitative evidence or properly comparable quantitative measures rather than surface-level arithmetic that creates illusion of precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use qualitative signs to judge taxation's burden on prosperity
rubrics_metrics.description: In absence of positive documents, form an opinion about taxation's relation to prosperity by observing: whether external appearance is flourishing; whether after taxes the poor retains means of subsistence and the rich means of enjoyment; and whether both classes are contented yet striving so industry is neither short of capital nor capital unemployed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess visible social indicators (general prosperity, subsistence of poor, enjoyment of rich, contentment and ongoing industry) as proxies for whether taxation is proportionate to real prosperity when reliable fiscal comparators are unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider geographical and security contexts in fiscal assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: A nation on the continent must maintain a large standing army and fleet (France) whereas an isolated republic (United States) may require far fewer forces; therefore inhabitants of differently situated states cannot be called upon to contribute equally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In fiscal comparisons factor in defense needs, exposure to invasion, and naval requirements which drive different levels of public expenditure and debt; failing to do so produces misleading comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate governmental economy by internal administrative practices
rubrics_metrics.description: If governments lack perseverance in undertakings and exercise no steady control over employees, they will often spend public money to no purpose or consume more than necessary. Democratic governments may devote large sums to satisfying lower orders, public instruction, remuneration of many services, and pay subordinate agents liberally, making them expensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine bureaucratic discipline, oversight, permanence of administrative practices, and incentives (salaries vs perquisites). Assess whether expenditures reflect purposeful public investment or inefficiency caused by weak control and short-termism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect democratic governments to tend toward higher expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever the poor direct public affairs and dispose of the national resources, they are apt to augment expenditure; thus the democratic government of the Americans is not a cheap government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forecasting budgetary trends in a democracy, account for political pressures to expand spending on popular benefits, education, and remuneration that arise from the composition of political power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish forms of corruption and their effects by regime type
rubrics_metrics.description: In aristocracies rulers sometimes endeavor to corrupt the people (buy voters); in democracies rulers frequently show themselves to be corrupt (public officers' probity questioned). In aristocracies the vices of rulers are directly prejudicial to people's morality; in democracies their indirect influence is more pernicious because it lends authority to base practices and is contagious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing corruption, consider both direct bribery and the subtler legitimizing effect of rulers' corruption on public morals. Evaluate how visibility and social proximity of corrupt behavior affect its spread among the populace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess social consequences of elite rise and perceptions of success
rubrics_metrics.description: In a democracy private citizens see peers rise to power rapidly; this can lead them to impute success to defects (low intrigues, immoral practices) and form an 'odious mixture' of turpitude and power, unworthiness and success, which discourages virtuous independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how the observable pathways to power in a regime shape norms: visible cases of rapid enrichment by public office can normalize corrupt ambition and erode civic virtue among social equals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate a democracy’s capacity for sustained national effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy is better adapted for occasional efforts of remarkable vigor (enthusiasm) than for hardy, prolonged endurance; enthusiasm prompts men to expose themselves to danger, but perseverance depends on distinct perception of the future which democracies often lack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether a polity can sustain long-term sacrifices (large-scale taxation, mass conscription, prolonged wars) by examining institutional mechanisms (conscription laws, willingness to adopt impressment, naval manpower systems), public temperament, and foresight rather than initial enthusiasm alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge democratic self-control in enacting and obeying laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The people are slow or frequently do not acquiesce in what is beneficial; legislation made by the people favors those classes most interested in evading it. Laws imposing privation or 'offensive' measures may not be enacted or obeyed (examples: no law against fraudulent bankruptcies, difficulty imposing duties on brandy, frontier justice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating legal reform prospects in a democracy, assess popular tolerance for privation, the distribution of interests among voters, and cultural habits that impede enactment or enforcement (e.g., tolerance of fraudulent bankruptcy, resistance to alcohol duties, prevalence of duels/fighting in frontier regions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess suitability of regime for foreign policy responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign politics demand qualities (secrecy, perseverance, patient execution, combination of measures) in which democracies are often deficient; consequently democratic foreign policy tends toward abstention and neutrality rather than ambitious, sustained external action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the regime can maintain secrecy, long-term planning, and patient execution in external affairs. Consider institutional delegation (executive and senate powers) and founding principles (Washington/Jefferson avoidance of entangling alliances, refusal to solicit foreign privileges) as markers of appropriate democratic foreign policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize long-term advantages of democracy despite short-term defects
rubrics_metrics.description: The defects of democratic government are easy to discover; its beneficial influence is less perceptible and only discerned by long observation. Democracy tends to increase the real strength of society over time—more populous, more prosperous—though it may be more frequently conquered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a democratic regime, weigh immediate visible flaws (defective laws, frequent change) against longer-term societal benefits such as diffusion of independence, growth of public spirit, increased respect for law, and expanded internal resources. Allow sufficient temporal horizon to observe these effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition reformability on public education and civic capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: A democracy can repair its faults only if it has attained a certain pitch of knowledge and civilization; some peoples are so viciously educated or ignorant that they cannot discern or accept remedies (examples: extinct or declining Indian tribes; tumultuous South American provinces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess prospects for corrective reform by examining levels of public education, civic habits, and social capacity to translate experience into improved institutions. In contexts lacking these, external remedies or force may be required (and may be problematic).
